summary: This unit teaches you to use a computer for everyday work tasks. You will learn to set up a safe workstation, start and shut down the computer, organise files and folders, write, format and print documents, build simple spreadsheets with formulas and charts, send email with attachments, search the internet, and keep your work and other people's information safe.

blocks.p: Almost every workplace now runs on computers. A fabrication shop types quotations and invoices and keeps a stock list; an electrical contractor emails customers and keeps job records; a villa keeps bookings, rosters and supply lists. This unit teaches the **basic computer applications** you need for that work: the word processor, the spreadsheet, email and the web browser, plus the file handling and safe habits that go with them.

**Who it is for:** this is a general unit in several Level 2 programmes, including Welding and Hospitality (villa and property services). You need no computer experience before you start. Menus and buttons differ a little between programs and versions; the ideas, and most keyboard shortcuts, are the same. Your instructor will show you the programs the Centre uses.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Set up the chair, screen, keyboard and mouse; take breaks; keep cables, plugs and drinks safe; clean and care for the equipment.
Name the main parts, input and output devices, storage and the operating system, and say what each does.
Start, use and shut down the computer
Log on, use the mouse, keyboard, desktop and windows, lock the screen, deal with a frozen program, and shut down properly.
Make folders, name, save, copy, move, rename, delete and find files, and back them up.
Type, edit, format, add tables, check spelling, set up the page, preview, save and print a document.
Enter data, write formulas and functions, copy them, format numbers, sort, chart and print.
Write, address, attach, send, reply to and file work emails, and spot fake ones.
Search for work information with good keywords and check that it can be trusted.
Keep information safe and solve simple problems
Use passwords, locking, antivirus and backups; fix simple faults such as a printer that will not print; report the rest.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on safe workstations, computer parts, files, word processing, spreadsheets, email, the internet, security and simple faults.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as icon, double-click, template, range, cursor, URL, inbox, CPU, hard copy) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Practical tasks**: creating, formatting and printing a one-page work notice with a table; and building a supplies cost list in a spreadsheet and sending it by email.

blocks.note: Keyboard shortcuts in this kit are for Windows computers, which most offices use. On an Apple Mac, use the Cmd key where this kit says Ctrl.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: A safe workstation and care of the equipment

blocks.p: Sitting at a computer looks safe, but hours of poor posture and staring at a screen cause **eye strain, headaches, neck and back pain, and aching wrists and hands**. Cables, plugs and spilt drinks bring trips, damage and electric shock. A few minutes of set-up prevents most of it.

head: Check
Good set-up
rows: Feet flat on the floor or a footrest; knees about level with your hips; lower back supported by the backrest
Straight in front of you, about an arm's length away, with the top at or a little below eye level; no glare from windows or lights
Close to you, so your elbows stay by your sides and your wrists stay straight
Within easy reach, so you do not twist or stretch
Tidy and off the floor where people walk
Away from the computer and keyboard

ul: Look away from the screen every 20 minutes or so, at something far away, to rest your eyes, and blink often.
Take short breaks: stand, stretch and walk for a few minutes at least once an hour.
If you still get pain or headaches, tell your supervisor: a footrest, a raised screen or a different mouse may solve it.
Check plugs, cables and power strips before use; report and stop using anything damaged.
Never overload a power strip or plug one power strip into another.
Use a **surge protector** or a **UPS** (uninterruptible power supply, a battery that keeps the computer running for a few minutes in a power cut) where one is provided.
Never open the computer's case or reach inside a printer beyond what the maker's instructions allow.

blocks.note: Power cuts and lightning surges are common in many parts of Jamaica. Save your work often (Ctrl + S), turn on automatic saving where the program has it, and in a thunderstorm follow the workplace's rule on switching off and unplugging.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Save your work, shut the computer down and switch off at the wall
Wipe the screen gently with a soft, dry, lint-free cloth; never spray liquid onto it or use paper towels
Turn the keyboard over and shake out crumbs gently; wipe the keys and mouse with a slightly damp cloth or a wipe made for electronics
Keep the air vents clear of dust, papers and walls, so the computer does not overheat
Report damage, burning smells, strange noises or overheating to your supervisor instead of opening the case

blocks.note: Keep office computers out of the workshop, away from welding, grinding dust, damp and direct sun. Grinding dust and fine metal particles get inside and can short-circuit the parts.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Hardware** is the parts you can touch. **Software** is the programs that make the hardware do useful work. The main program, which runs the computer, manages files and lets other programs work, is the **operating system** (for example Windows, macOS or Linux; on phones, Android or iOS). The programs you use for tasks, such as a word processor, are **applications**.

head: Kind of device
What it does
Examples
rows: Puts information or commands into the computer
Keyboard, mouse, touchpad, scanner, microphone, webcam, barcode reader
Shows or gives out information from the computer
The **CPU** (central processing unit, the processor): the computer's "brain"
Holds the programs and work in use, while the computer is on
**RAM**: fast, but emptied when the power goes off
Keeps files when the computer is off
Hard disk drive (HDD) or solid-state drive (SSD) inside; USB flash drive, memory card, external drive; cloud storage online

blocks.p: A touch screen is both an input device (you touch it) and an output device (it shows you things).

blocks.note: While you work, your document is held in **RAM**, which is cleared the moment the power goes off. Only what has been **saved** to storage survives a power cut or a crash. That is why you save early and often.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Unit
About
Holds roughly
rows: A photo, or a long document with pictures
Thousands of photos; a USB flash drive is often 16 to 128 GB

ul: **USB** ports connect flash drives, keyboards, mice, printers and phones.
**HDMI** (or a similar video port) connects a monitor or projector.
A **network** (Ethernet) port or Wi-Fi connects the computer to the office network and the internet.

head: Application
Used for
Work examples
rows: Letters, quotations, notices, rosters, reports, job sheets
Tables of numbers with calculations and charts
Price lists, stock lists, cost sheets, timesheets, budgets
Slides for a talk or a screen display
A toolbox talk on safety; a show of past jobs for a customer
Sending and receiving messages and files
Opening and viewing pages on the internet
Supplier prices, product data sheets, online forms
Opening, viewing and printing PDF files

sections.title: Starting, using and shutting down the computer

flow: Check the cables and that the area is safe; switch on at the wall, then press the computer's power button
Log on with your own username and password
The **desktop** appears: the main screen, with icons, the taskbar and the start menu
Open a program by clicking its icon in the start menu or taskbar, or double-clicking an icon on the desktop

head: Action
How
What it does
rows: Selects an item or presses a button
Press the left button twice quickly
Opens a file, folder or program
Shows a short menu of options for that item
Hold the left button down and move
Moves an item, or selects text
Moves up and down a page

blocks.p: Each open program or folder shows in a **window**. The buttons at the top right **minimise** it (hide it on the taskbar), **maximise** it (fill the screen) or **close** it (X). The taskbar shows every open window, so you can switch between them. An **icon** is a small picture that stands for a program, file or folder. The **cursor** is the flashing line in a document that shows where the next letter will appear; the mouse **pointer** is the arrow.

head: Key
What it does
rows: Hold it down and press a letter to type one capital letter, or the top symbol on a key
Turns capital letters on for every letter until pressed again; a light often shows when it is on
Starts a new paragraph in a document, or confirms a choice
Deletes the character to the left of the cursor
Deletes the character to the right of the cursor, or the selected item
Jumps to the next tab stop, or the next box or table cell
Move the cursor up, down, left and right
Cancels or closes a menu or box
Used with other keys for shortcuts

head: Shortcut (Windows)
What it does
rows: Undo the last action / redo it
Cut the selection (remove it, ready to paste)
Ctrl + B / Ctrl + I / Ctrl + U

head: Option
What it does
When to use it
rows: Hides your work behind the log-on screen; everything stays open
Whenever you leave the desk, even for a minute
Closes your programs and your session; the computer stays on for the next person
At the end of your shift on a shared computer
After updates, or when the computer is slow or misbehaving
Closes everything and turns the computer off safely
At the end of the day, as the workplace's rules say

ul: Before you shut down, **save your work and close your programs**, then choose Shut down from the start menu.
Never just pull the plug or switch off at the wall while the computer is running: open files can be damaged and unsaved work is lost.
Holding the power button down until the computer goes off is a last resort for a computer that is completely frozen.

flow: Wait a minute: the program may be busy, for example saving or printing
Try to close it normally with the X
If it still will not close, press Ctrl + Alt + Delete, open Task Manager, select the program and choose End task
Restart the computer if things are still slow; report it if it keeps happening

blocks.p: A **file** is one saved piece of work: a letter, a spreadsheet, a photo. A **folder** holds files that belong together, and can hold other folders. A good folder structure means anyone can find a file in seconds.

head: Folder
Inside it (fabrication shop)
Inside it (villa)
rows: Quotations, Invoices, Job sheets, Staff rosters, Suppliers
Bookings, Housekeeping, Maintenance, Supplies, Staff rosters
Folders for each year, such as 2026
Folders for each year or month

ul: A good file name says **what the file is** and **the date**: "2026-11-03 Quote - Lewis gate" or "Housekeeping roster - Nov 2026".
Writing the date as **year-month-day** (2026-11-03) makes files sort in date order.
Never leave a name such as "Document1" or "new final final". Keep one current version, not five copies with similar names.
Windows will not accept these characters in a file name: \ / : * ? " < > |

blocks.p: The letters after the dot in a file name, the **extension**, show the type of file and which program opens it.

head: Extension
Type of file
rows: PDF: looks the same on any device and is hard to change; good for sending quotations and invoices
Plain table of data that any spreadsheet can open
Several files squeezed into one smaller file
A program that installs or runs. Never open one from an unknown email, website or USB drive.

head: Task
How
rows: Ctrl + S, or File > Save. The first time, choose the folder and type the name.
Saves a **copy with a new name or in a new place**; the original stays as it was
Right-click > Copy, go to the new folder, right-click > Paste. The file is now in **two** places.
Right-click > Cut, then Paste in the new folder. The file is now in **one** place, the new one.
Right-click > Rename, type the new name, press Enter. Keep the extension.
Select it and press Delete. Files deleted from the computer's own drive go to the **Recycle Bin**, where they can be restored until it is emptied.
Type part of the file name in the search box of the file window or the start menu

blocks.note: Files deleted from a **USB flash drive** or a network drive usually do **not** go to the Recycle Bin: they are gone for good. Think twice before deleting from these.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Before you pull out a flash drive, close the files on it and choose **Eject** (or Safely remove). Pulling it out while files are being copied or are open can damage them.
Do not plug in a flash drive you found or were given by a stranger: it can carry a virus.
Do not carry customers' or guests' details on a personal flash drive.

head: Place
Good point
Weak point
rows: Quick, and works without the internet
Lost if the computer breaks, is stolen or gets a virus; others cannot reach the files
Small, cheap, easy to carry between computers
Easily lost or damaged; can spread viruses; anyone who finds it can read it
Kept away from the building, safe if the computer fails; the team can reach it from anywhere
Needs the internet and a strong, secret password

blocks.p: A **backup** is a second copy kept in another place. Important work should always be in **more than one place**, and the backup should be updated regularly and checked from time to time.

ul: Start a new blank document, or a **template**: a ready-made document with a set layout, such as a blank invoice, that you fill in each time.
Just keep typing at the end of a line: the text wraps by itself. Press **Enter** only to start a new paragraph.
To change text, first **select** it: drag across it, double-click a word, or click at the start and Shift + click at the end.
Copy and paste: select the text, **copy** (Ctrl + C), click where it is to go, **paste** (Ctrl + V). Cut (Ctrl + X) instead of copy to move it.
Made a mistake? **Undo** (Ctrl + Z) reverses your last action, even a deleted paragraph.
**Find and Replace** (often Ctrl + H) changes a word everywhere at once, for example every "Cottage" to "Garden Suite".

head: Format
What it does
Use it for
rows: The style and size of the letters, in points (pt)
A clear font; body text about 11 to 12 pt; headings bigger
Headings and the few words that must stand out
Names of documents, or a gentle stress
Use little: it can look like a web link
Left, centre, right or justified (both edges straight)
Centre a heading; keep body text left-aligned
Bullets for items in any order; numbers for steps in order
A little extra space makes a notice easier to read

blocks.note: To centre a heading, select it and click the **Centre** alignment button. Do not push it across with spaces: it will not line up, and it moves if the text changes.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Use a **table** to line up information in rows and columns, such as day, task, person and time on a roster, or item, quantity and price on a list. Never line things up with spaces.
Insert the table with the number of columns you need; make the heading row bold.
Press **Tab** to move to the next cell; pressing Tab in the last cell adds a new row.
Adjust column widths so the text fits, and add or remove borders as needed.

head: Setting
What it controls
rows: **Portrait** (tall) or **landscape** (wide). Landscape suits wide tables and charts.
Must match the paper in the printer: **Letter** (216 × 279 mm) or **A4** (210 × 297 mm), and sometimes Legal (216 × 356 mm)
The blank space round the edge of the page
Text that repeats at the top or bottom of **every page**: a business name, a title, the date
Inserted in the header or footer; they update themselves

blocks.note: Many offices in Jamaica use **Letter** paper, while many programs start new documents on A4, or the other way round. If a document is set to the wrong size, the printer may stop and ask for paper, shrink the page, or cut off the bottom lines. Set the paper size in the document to match the paper in the printer.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: A **red wavy line** under a word means it may be **spelt wrong** or is not in the dictionary. A blue or green line marks a possible grammar problem. Right-click for suggestions.
Set the checking language to English (UK) or English (Jamaica), so that words like colour and centre are not marked wrong.
The spell checker cannot find a real word in the wrong place (from/form, there/their, now/not). **Proofread** it yourself, and check names, dates, times, prices and phone numbers.

flow: Save the document
Open **Print Preview** (in many programs, File > Print shows it) to see how the pages will look before using paper
Choose the printer, the number of copies, and which pages (all, the current page, or a range such as 1-3)
Choose one-sided or two-sided, and check the paper size and orientation
Print, then check the printout (the **hard copy**) before handing it out

blocks.p: To send a document that the reader must not change, such as a quotation, save it (or export it) as a **PDF**.
A spreadsheet is a grid for numbers and calculations. A spreadsheet file is a **workbook**; it holds one or more **worksheets** (sheets), shown as tabs at the bottom.

head: Term
What it means
rows: Runs down the sheet; named by letters: A, B, C ...
Runs across the sheet; named by numbers: 1, 2, 3 ...
One box, where a column and a row meet
The column letter then the row number: **C4** is column C, row 4
A group of cells chosen together, written with a colon: **B2:B6** means B2, B3, B4, B5 and B6
The cell you are working in, shown with a thick border
Shows what is really in the active cell, such as the formula behind a total

ul: Every formula starts with an **equals sign (=)**.
Use cell references, not the numbers themselves, so the answer **updates by itself** when a number changes.
The signs are: **+** add, **-** subtract, ***** multiply, **/** divide.
Brackets are worked out first: =(B2+C2)*2 adds B2 and C2, then doubles the result.

head: Function
What it does
Example
rows: Finds the average (mean) of a range
Finds the largest number in a range
Finds the smallest number in a range
Counts how many cells in a range hold numbers

blocks.h: Worked example: a supplies cost list

flow: Type the headings in row 1 and make them bold
Type one item per row, with its quantity and the price of one unit
In D2 type =B2*C2 and press Enter
Copy D2 down the column: drag the small square at the bottom-right corner of the cell (the **fill handle**), or copy and paste
Under the last item, type Total and use =SUM for the Cost column
Format the money cells with two decimal places (or as currency), and widen columns so everything shows
Check two or three answers with a calculator, then save with a clear name

blocks.note: When you copy a formula down, its cell references change to match the new row: =B2*C2 in row 2 becomes =B3*C3 in row 3. That is why one formula can be copied down a whole list. To keep a reference fixed, such as a cell holding the GCT rate, put $ signs in it: =D2*$F$1 always uses F1, wherever it is copied.
blocks.label: Remember

head: You see
It usually means
Fix
rows: The column is too narrow to show the number
The formula divides by zero or an empty cell
Check the cell it divides by
The formula tries to do sums with text
Check that the cells hold numbers, not words or spaces
The function name is spelt wrong
Correct the spelling, for example SUM not SUMM
A cell the formula used has been deleted

ul: **Sort** puts rows in order: A to Z, Z to A, smallest to largest.
Select the **whole table** (or click inside it) before sorting, so each row stays together. Sorting one column on its own separates names from their numbers.
**Filter** hides the rows you do not want for now, for example to show only one supplier's items.

head: Chart
Best for
Example
rows: Cost of each item on the list
Showing how one whole is split into parts
How a month's budget splits into wages, materials and electricity
Spending on materials each month for six months

ul: Select the data, including the headings, then choose Insert > Chart and the type.
Give the chart a clear title, and label the axes with units (J$, months).
Use Print Preview: a sheet can spill onto many pages.
Choose landscape for wide sheets, and "fit all columns on one page" so no column prints on a page by itself.
Set a print area if you only need part of the sheet.

head: Part
What goes in it
rows: The main person (or people) the email is for. Check the address carefully: the program may fill in the wrong person.
People who need a copy to stay informed; everyone can see who was copied
People who get a copy **without** the others seeing their address. Use it when emailing many customers at once, to keep their addresses private.
A short, clear summary: "Quotation for burglar bars - 14 Hope Road"
Greeting, a short polite message, and a sign-off
A file sent with the email, shown with a paper-clip sign
Your name, job title, business and phone number at the end

head: Button
Sends to
rows: Only the person who sent the email
The sender and everyone else in To and CC. Use it when they all need your answer.
Someone new, with the email (and its attachments) included

blocks.p: Email folders: the **inbox** (new messages arrive here), **sent** (copies of what you sent), **drafts** (unfinished emails), **junk or spam** (emails the program thinks are unwanted) and **deleted items** (the bin). Make folders for jobs or customers and file emails once they are dealt with.

blocks.h: Writing and sending a work email

flow: Click New message and type the address in To; add CC or BCC if needed
Write a clear subject line
Greet the reader, say what you need in a few short sentences, and sign off with your name and contact details
Attach the file, and check that the right file is attached
Read it all again: address, spelling, tone, facts
Send, then check the Sent folder

ul: Many email services limit attachments to about 20 to 25 MB per email. For many photos or large files, send a link from the workplace's cloud storage, or send them in smaller batches.
Do not write in capitals, use text slang, or send angry emails. Read it again in the morning if you are upset.
Do not send customers' or guests' details to people who do not need them.
A **web browser** is the program that opens web pages. A **search engine** is a website, opened in the browser, that finds pages for you.
A web address is called a **URL**, such as www.example.com. Type it in the address bar at the top of the browser.
Search with a few clear **keywords**, including the place: "square steel tube supplier Kingston" works better than "where can I buy steel please".
Put words in quotation marks to search for that exact phrase.
Save useful pages as **bookmarks** (favourites) to find them again.

head: Check
Good signs
rows: A real business or official body, with a street address and phone number
Prices and news with recent dates
In Jamaican dollars, saying whether GCT is included
Correct spelling; no flood of pop-up adverts; offers that are not far too good to be true
Two or three suppliers compared; the price confirmed by phone before ordering

blocks.note: The padlock and "https" at the start of the address mean the connection is **encrypted**, so others cannot read what passes between you and the site. It does **not** prove the business is real or honest: scam sites can have a padlock too.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Download files only from websites you trust, and never run a program (.exe) downloaded from an unknown site. Ask your supervisor or IT support first.
Write down where information came from: the website address and the date, so your supervisor can check it.

sections.title: Keeping information safe and solving problems

head: Habit
Why
rows: Log on with your **own account** and keep your password secret
Your work is yours, and nobody can act in your name
Use a **strong password**: long, with a mix of letters, numbers and symbols, not a name or birthday
Short and obvious passwords are guessed in seconds
**Lock** the screen whenever you leave the desk; **sign out** at the end of the shift
Stops others using your account or reading customer details
They find and remove viruses and close security holes
Do not open strange emails, links or attachments, or plug in unknown USB drives
These are the main ways viruses and scams get in
Keep customer and guest details only in the proper folders, not on the desktop or a personal drive
Protects people's privacy, as Jamaica's data protection law expects
Work survives a crash, theft or virus
Report problems at once: a lost flash drive, a suspected scam, a virus warning

ul: Warning signs: an urgent threat ("your account will close today"), a request to click a link and type your password or bank details, a sender's address that does not match the company, spelling mistakes, and unexpected attachments.
Hover the mouse pointer over a link (without clicking) to see the real address it goes to.
Do not click, reply or open attachments. Report it to your supervisor or IT support and delete it.

blocks.h: When the printer will not print

flow: Check that you sent the job to the right printer: the computer may be set to a different one
Check the printer is switched on, and look for an error message or light
Check the power cable, and the USB or network cable or the Wi-Fi connection
Check there is paper of the right size in the tray, and no paper jam; clear a jam only as the maker's instructions say, with the printer switched off
Check the ink or toner level
Open the print queue on the computer; cancel a stuck job and try again
Still not working, or an error you do not understand? Stop, do not open the printer's inside, and report it to your supervisor

head: Problem
Try this
rows: Your password is right but will not work
Check Caps Lock is off and the keyboard language is right; ask the supervisor to reset it if it is locked
Close programs you are not using; save and restart
Check its extension and that you have the right program; ask before installing anything
Use the search box with part of the name; look in Recent files and the Downloads folder
A file was deleted by mistake
Look in the Recycle Bin and choose Restore; files deleted from USB drives cannot be restored this way
Check the Wi-Fi or network cable; restart the computer; ask whether others are affected, then report it

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it at a computer.

ul: I can set up a workstation to avoid strain, and keep cables, plugs and drinks safe.
I can clean and care for computer equipment safely.
I can name input, output, processing, memory and storage devices, and explain the operating system.
I can explain why unsaved work is lost in a power cut.
I can log on, use the mouse and keyboard, lock the screen, sign out and shut down properly.
I can deal with a program that stops responding.
I can make folders, and name, save, copy, move, rename, delete, find and back up files.
I can explain Save and Save As, and what different file extensions mean.
I can type, edit, copy and paste, undo, and find and replace text.
I can format text, headings and lists, and insert and fill in a table.
I can set the orientation, paper size, margins, header and footer.
I can check spelling and proofread a document.
I can preview, print and save a document as a PDF.
I can enter data in a spreadsheet and write formulas with +, -, *, / and SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN and COUNT.
I can copy a formula down a column, and fix a reference with $ when I need to.
I can format numbers, sort a table, make a suitable chart and print a sheet.
I can write, address, attach, send, reply to and file a work email, and use CC and BCC correctly.
I can search the internet with good keywords and check that a website can be trusted.
I can keep information safe and spot a phishing email.
I can work through the checks when a printer will not print, and report what I cannot fix.

terms: Antivirus
A program that finds and removes viruses and other harmful software
Application
A program used for a task, such as a word processor or spreadsheet
Attachment
A file sent with an email
BCC
Blind carbon copy: sends a copy without other people seeing that address
Backup
A second copy of files kept in another place
CC
Carbon copy: sends a copy to someone who needs to know
Cell reference
The column letter and row number of a cell, such as C4
CPU
Central processing unit: the processor, the computer's "brain"
Cursor
The flashing line that shows where the next letter will appear
Desktop
The main screen you see after you log on
Double-click
Pressing the left mouse button twice quickly
Extension
The letters after the dot in a file name, showing the file type
Folder
A place that holds files that belong together
Formula
A calculation in a spreadsheet cell, starting with =
Hard copy
A copy on paper; a printout
Icon
A small picture that stands for a program, file or folder
Inbox
The email folder where new messages arrive
Operating system
The main program that runs the computer
Print Preview
A view of how the pages will look when printed
RAM
The computer's working memory, emptied when the power goes off
Range
A group of cells chosen together, such as B2:B6
Recycle Bin
Where files deleted from the computer's drive go until it is emptied
Search engine
A website that finds web pages from keywords
Template
A ready-made document with a set layout, filled in each time
URL
The address of a web page
USB flash drive
A small, portable storage device that plugs into a USB port
Web browser
The program used to open and view web pages
Word processor
A program for typing, formatting and printing documents
Workbook
A spreadsheet file, holding one or more worksheets

c1.title: A cost sheet at a fabrication shop in Spanish Town
c1.text: Nadine is the office assistant at a steel fabrication shop in Spanish Town, St Catherine. She is building a spreadsheet of safety and welding supplies. Row 1 holds the headings: A Item, B Quantity, C Unit price (J$), D Cost. Rows 2 to 5 hold: electrodes (boxes) 4 at 6,500; grinding discs 25 at 450; welding gloves (pairs) 6 at 1,800; safety glasses 10 at 650. D2 holds the formula =B2*C2. Cell F1 holds the GCT rate. On another sheet she keeps the shop's spending on electrodes for each month from January to June.

c2.title: A cleaning roster at a villa near Duncans
c2.text: Miss Hylton, the housekeeping supervisor at a villa near Duncans, Trelawny, is typing a three-page cleaning roster and notice for staff. She wants the villa's name and "Housekeeping Roster - December" at the top of every page. The office printer is loaded with Letter paper, but the document is set to A4, and the last line of each page is not printing. The villa has also renamed the Cottage the Garden Suite, and the old name appears many times in the document.

c3.title: Files in a site office in Morant Bay
c3.text: Dwight works in the site office of a contractor in Morant Bay, St Thomas. His files are saved on the desktop with names like Document1, Quote new final and Lewis gate 3 Nov. He copies quotations to a USB flash drive to print them at the main office. Yesterday he deleted an old quotation from the flash drive, and now he needs it back. He also cannot remember which folder he saved this week's job list in.

c4.title: Emails from an electrical contractor in Black River
c4.text: Tanisha handles the email for an electrical contractor in Black River, St Elizabeth. She sends a quotation to a customer with her supervisor in CC, and the customer replies with a question about the price. She must also email a notice about new opening hours to 30 customers, and send a customer 40 MB of photos of a finished rewiring job.

c5.title: Searching for suppliers from Junction
c5.text: Kemoy works at a small welding shop in Junction, St Elizabeth. His supervisor asks him to find prices for 25 mm square steel tube from suppliers in Kingston and Mandeville. One website has no address or phone number, shows prices from three years ago, and offers a "free price calculator" program to download. The site's address starts with https and shows a padlock.

questions.q: Nadine copies the formula in D2 down to D3. What formula will D3 hold?
questions.why: Cell references in a copied formula move with it: one row down, B2 and C2 become B3 and C3. That is why one formula can be copied down the whole list.

questions.q: In D6 Nadine types =SUM(D2:D5). What should the cell show?
questions.why: The costs are 26,000 + 11,250 + 10,800 + 6,500 = 54,550. 45 is the total of the quantities and 9,400 is the total of the unit prices, neither of which is the cost.

questions.q: She wants the GCT on each line in column E, using the rate in F1, and will copy the first formula down. Which should she type in E2?
o: =SUM(D2:F1)
questions.why: The $ signs keep F1 fixed when the formula is copied, while D2 changes to D3, D4 and so on. Without them, the copied formulas would look at F2, F3 and F4, which are empty.

questions.q: Which chart best shows whether the shop's spending on electrodes rose or fell from January to June?
o: A pie chart with one slice for each of the months
A single column showing the six-month total
A pie chart of the different items bought in June
A line chart, months along the bottom
questions.why: A line chart shows change over time, so a rise or fall is easy to see. A pie chart shows parts of one whole, and a single total hides the changes.

questions.q: How should Miss Hylton put the villa's name and the title at the top of every page?
o: Type them at the top of each page by hand
Put them in the header
Make them bold and centred on page 1
Insert them as a table on each page
questions.why: A header repeats on every page by itself and stays in place when the text moves. Typing it on each page by hand goes wrong as soon as lines are added or removed.

questions.q: Why is the last line of each page not printing?
o: The font is too large for the page margins
The printer cannot handle three-page jobs
The document is A4 but the paper is Letter
The ink cartridge is running very low
questions.why: A4 is about 18 mm longer than Letter, so text near the bottom of an A4 page falls off a Letter sheet. She should set the document's paper size to Letter, to match the printer.

questions.q: What is the quickest reliable way to change every "Cottage" to "Garden Suite"?
o: Use Find and Replace
Read through and retype each one
Use the spell checker
Copy and paste each one
questions.why: Find and Replace changes every match in one go, and can show each one first. The spell checker will not help, because "Cottage" is spelt correctly.

questions.q: Which file name is best for this week's quotation for Mr Lewis's gate?
o: Quote new final - Lewis gate
Lewis gate quote 3 Nov final
Document1 - Lewis gate copy
2026-11-03 Lewis gate quote
questions.why: It says what the file is and gives the date as year-month-day, so quotations sort in date order and the newest is easy to find. "New", "final" and "copy" mean nothing a week later.

questions.q: What should Dwight do before he pulls the flash drive out of the computer?
o: Close its files and choose Eject
Switch the computer off at the wall first
Rename the drive with today's date
Empty the computer's Recycle Bin first
questions.why: Pulling a drive out while files are open or still copying can damage them. Eject (Safely remove) tells the computer to finish and let go of the drive.

questions.q: Why can Dwight not find the deleted quotation in the Recycle Bin?
o: The Recycle Bin empties itself at midnight
Quotations are never kept in the Recycle Bin
Deleted flash drive files usually skip it
The flash drive was not plugged in long enough
questions.why: Only files deleted from the computer's own drive go to the Recycle Bin. Files deleted from a flash drive or network drive are usually gone for good, which is one reason to keep backups.

questions.q: How can Dwight quickly find this week's job list?
o: Open every folder on the computer in turn
Type part of its name in the search box
Restart the computer so the file appears
Make a new job list and type it again
questions.why: The search box in the file window or start menu looks through the folders for files whose name contains the words you type. Then move the file to the right folder.

questions.q: How should Tanisha address the notice to the 30 customers?
o: Put all 30 addresses in the To box
Put all 30 addresses in the CC box
Send one email and ask them to share it
Put all 30 addresses in the BCC box
questions.why: BCC sends each customer a copy without showing them the other 29 addresses, which keeps customers' details private. Addresses in To or CC are seen by everyone; her own address can go in To.

questions.q: The customer replies to the quotation with a question. The supervisor must stay informed. How should Tanisha answer?
o: Reply all, so the supervisor sees it too
Reply, so that only the customer gets the answer
Forward the email to the customer with her answer
Start a new email to the customer with no subject
questions.why: Reply all goes to the sender and everyone in To and CC, so the supervisor stays in the conversation. Reply alone would leave the supervisor out.

questions.q: The 40 MB of photos will not send as attachments. What should she do?
o: Send them as one email again later
Share a link from cloud storage
Print the photos and post them
Send only the first photo instead
questions.why: Many email services limit attachments to about 20 to 25 MB. A link from the workplace's cloud storage, or several smaller emails, gets all the photos to the customer.

questions.q: Which supplier website is most likely to be a real local business?
o: One with an address, phone and current J$ prices
One with lots of colourful adverts and pop-up boxes
One that offers prices far below everyone else's
One that appears first in the list of search results
questions.why: A real business gives a way to find and call it, and keeps its prices current. Adverts, very low prices and the top search position do not prove a business is real; many top results are paid adverts.

questions.q: What does the padlock and "https" on the website tell Kemoy?
o: The business has been checked by the government
The prices on the site are up to date
The connection to the site is encrypted
The download on the site is free of viruses
questions.why: The padlock shows only that the connection is encrypted. Scam sites can have one too, so it says nothing about whether the business or its downloads can be trusted.

questions.q: What should Kemoy do about the "free price calculator" download?
o: Download it but run it only once
Leave it, and tell his supervisor
Download it onto a flash drive first
Download it if the file is very small
questions.why: A program from an unknown site, with no address and old prices, may carry a virus. Programs are installed only from trusted sources, with the supervisor's or IT's permission.

questions.q: Dahlia types her password carefully, but the computer keeps saying it is wrong. What should she check first?
o: That the screen brightness is high enough
That the mouse is plugged in properly
That Caps Lock has not been left on
That the printer is switched on
questions.why: Passwords are case-sensitive, so with Caps Lock on every letter is typed as a capital. Check the light or the on-screen warning, then type it again.

questions.q: The power goes off while Kirk is typing a report he has not saved for an hour. Why is that hour's work lost?
o: The keyboard deleted the words when the power failed
It was only in RAM, which empties with no power
The printer had not yet printed the report
The screen keeps only the last page shown
questions.why: Work in progress lives in RAM until it is saved to the drive, and RAM is cleared when the power goes. Saving every few minutes, and a UPS, protect against this.

questions.q: Shauna-Lee sorted only the Name column of a timesheet A to Z, and now the hours no longer match the names. What went wrong?
o: The names were typed in capital letters
She should have sorted Z to A instead
The hours column was too narrow to show
Sorting one column split the rows
questions.why: Sorting one column moves only that column, splitting each row. Select the whole table (or click inside it) so the sort moves every row together. Undo (Ctrl + Z) will put it back.
